name: Sensor and Shipping Data
title: Sensor and Shipping Data
answer: Sensor and shipping data covers the physical signals that track goods and vessels as they move: automatic identification system (AIS) broadcasts from ships, port call records, container and terminal throughput, satellite imagery of vessels and storage tanks, and telemetry from trucks, rail and warehouse equipment. In alternative data terms it sits alongside card transactions and web scraping as a source of near real time economic activity, used mainly to estimate trade volumes, freight rates, inventories and retail demand before official statistics appear. The scope runs from raw positional pings to derived measures such as port congestion indices and vessel waiting times.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Sensor and shipping data covers the physical signals that track goods and vessels as they move: automatic identification system (AIS) broadcasts from ships, port call records, container and terminal throughput, satellite imagery of vessels and storage tanks, and telemetry from trucks, rail and warehouse equipment. In alternative data terms it sits alongside card transactions and web scraping as a source of near real time economic activity, used mainly to estimate trade volumes, freight rates, inventories and retail demand before official statistics appear. The scope runs from raw positional pings to derived measures such as port congestion indices and vessel waiting times.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The raw material is a continuous stream of timestamped positions and events, often millions of records a day, delivered by satellite and terrestrial receivers, port authorities, customs filings and logistics operators. Storage and processing typically sit in cloud object stores and columnar databases, with streaming pipelines for live feeds and batch jobs for historical backfill. Identity resolution is a core infrastructure problem, since the same vessel, container or company appears under different identifiers across sources, and coverage gaps appear where receivers are sparse or signals are switched off.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work begins with cleaning and geolocating the feeds, then joining them to reference data on vessels, ports, companies and routes. Analysts and data scientists build features such as dwell time, speed changes, route deviation and port arrivals, and use them in nowcasting models, anomaly detection and simple aggregations that are compared against official trade and freight series. Machine learning is used for tasks like vessel classification, destination prediction and detecting dark activity, while much of the day to day work remains careful data engineering and validation against known events.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights are layered and often restrictive: AIS is broadcast openly but redistributors assert database rights over cleaned histories, satellite imagery is licensed per scene, and port or customs records may be commercially confidential or personally identifying for crews. Contracts usually limit redistribution, require attribution and forbid use in identifying individuals, and some jurisdictions treat vessel tracking as a security matter. Provenance matters because a single mislabelled vessel or duplicated port call can distort a whole index, so vendors are expected to document sources, cleaning steps and known coverage limits, and buyers increasingly ask for audit trails before relying on the data.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Coverage is widening as more satellites, cheaper receivers and port digitalisation add sources, and as machine learning improves the automatic labelling of vessels, cargoes and routes. At the same time, signal interference, sanctions driven dark fleets and tighter rules on personal and security sensitive data are pushing vendors toward fusion of multiple feeds and clearer disclosure of uncertainty. The likely direction is fewer single source products and more composite activity measures that are validated against official statistics, with governance and provenance treated as part of the product rather than an afterthought.
